events.title: EDSAC Initial Orders — first working assembler
events.summary: David Wheeler's Initial Orders on EDSAC translated symbolic mnemonics into machine code — the first assembler program.
events.about: Assembly language sits one step above raw machine code: you write short mnemonics like `A 80` instead of 17-bit binary patterns. Wheeler's program ran at Cambridge on EDSAC and read symbolic instructions from paper tape. Every compiler, OS, and device driver chain since then starts from this idea.

narrative.whyChosen: Before assemblers, programmers punched binary instruction words by hand — one wrong bit broke the whole run.
narrative.whyImportant: Automating mnemonic-to-machine-code translation made programming repeatable and launched the software industry.
narrative.problemSolved: Human transcription of machine instructions was slow, error-prone, and did not scale as computers grew more capable.
